qs.q: Under what circumstance is a lumbar puncture strictly indicated for a child presenting with fever and a seizure?
o: Age younger than 6 months at presentation
Presence of a simple seizure lasting 5 minutes
Presence of a positive family seizure history
Occurrence of the initial seizure during sleep
qs.e: A lumbar puncture should be performed for all infants younger than 6 months of age who present with fever and seizure, or if the child is ill-appearing at any age. Meningitis must always be considered in the differential diagnosis.

qs.q: A 2-month-old infant presents with a sepsis-like syndrome and severe lesions of the cerebral cortex on brain MRI. Lumbar puncture demonstrates minimal CSF pleocytosis. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this presentation?
o: Human parechovirus infection
Herpes simplex virus type 1
Varicella-zoster virus infection
Cytomegalovirus brain infection
qs.e: Human parechovirus typically affects infants and presents with abdominal signs or a sepsis-like syndrome, severe cortical MRI lesions, and minimal or absent CSF pleocytosis. HSV-1 classically causes severe focal lesions in the temporal lobes rather than minimal pleocytosis with cortical lesions in infants.

qs.q: Why is it recommended that an experienced proceduralist perform the initial lumbar puncture in a child with suspected acute lymphoblastic leukaemia?
o: A traumatic lumbar puncture is associated with an increased risk of CNS relapse
Inexperienced operators frequently fail to measure opening pressures accurately
Intrathecal chemotherapy cannot be administered without direct surgical assistance
Traumatic lumbar punctures always cause immediate and severe systemic sepsis
qs.e: An experienced proceduralist should perform the initial LP because a traumatic LP is associated with an increased risk of CNS relapse. The text does not attribute failure of opening pressure measurement as the primary reason.

qs.q: When is a lumbar puncture strictly indicated in an infant or child presenting with a fever and a seizure?
o: In all children older than 24 months presenting with a simple seizure
In infants younger than 6 months, if ill-appearing, or if clinical concerns exist
Only when the patient has a known family history of generalized epilepsy
Whenever the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes regardless of appearance
qs.e: A lumbar puncture should be performed for all infants younger than 6 months presenting with fever and seizure, if the child is ill-appearing, or at any age if there are clinical signs of concern for meningitis. It is not routinely required for simple febrile seizures in older, well-appearing children.

qs.q: How should cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings be interpreted when a lumbar puncture is performed in a patient presenting with febrile status epilepticus?
o: Pleocytosis is universally present in over 90% of uncomplicated cases.
A nontraumatic lumbar puncture rarely shows pleocytosis, with 96% having under 3 cells.
Elevated CSF protein and glucose levels are required to confirm a viral etiology.
CSF findings will always show a marked decrease in glucose due to consumption.
qs.e: In patients with febrile status epilepticus, a nontraumatic lumbar puncture rarely shows CSF pleocytosis, with 96% having fewer than 3 nucleated cells and concurrently normal protein and glucose. Any significant pleocytosis should raise suspicion for a bacterial or viral CNS infection.

qs.q: According to American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommendations, when should a lumbar puncture be strongly considered in a child presenting with a seizure and fever?
o: When the child is less than 12 months
When the child has a normal examination
When routine blood test results are abnormal
When the seizure duration is brief
qs.e: Lumbar puncture should be strongly considered in febrile children under 12 months because meningeal signs are very subtle and difficult to identify at this age. In children older than 18 months or without fever, the indication is different.

qs.q: Which diagnostic specimen is specifically collected via a lumbar puncture to investigate central nervous system infections?
o: Sputum specimen
Blood specimen
Cerebrospinal fluid
Wound swab specimen
qs.e: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is the fluid around the brain and spinal cord collected via lumbar puncture for lab analysis. Sputum is collected for lung infections rather than central nervous system evaluations.

qs.q: During a lumbar puncture procedure, the clinician inserts a needle into the subarachnoid space. Below which vertebral level does the spinal cord typically terminate in an adult?
o: Vertebral level L1/L2
Vertebral level T12/L1
Vertebral level L3/L4
Vertebral level S1/S2
qs.e: The spinal cord terminates at the conus medullaris around the L1/L2 vertebral level, leaving the lumbar cistern safe for lumbar puncture. Terminations below L3 are atypical and outside normal anatomical landmarks.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A lumbar puncture (LP) is the gold standard for diagnosing meningitis and other central nervous system disorders. In resource‑limited hospitals, clinical judgment, basic CSF analysis, and rapid bedside tests guide management when advanced labs are unavailable.

sections.p: A lumbar puncture is the insertion of a needle into the lumbar subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for analysis. Diagnosis is based on CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen tests when available.
b: Technique: patient in lateral decubitus or sitting, lumbar region 1–2 vertebrae above the iliac crest, sterile field, local anaesthetic, 22‑25G needle

t.b: Measures intracranial pressure; >200 mmH2O suggests increased ICP, <80 mmH2O suggests low ICP
Differentiates bacterial (neutrophil predominance, >1000 cells/µL) from viral (lymphocyte predominance, 50–500 cells/µL) meningitis
Elevated in bacterial, TB, fungal meningitis; normal in viral
Low (<40 mg/dL or <2/3 serum) in bacterial/TB; normal in viral
Detects bacteria; positive in ~50% of bacterial meningitis
Positive in cryptococcal meningitis; useful when culture is delayed

sections.p: Severity is gauged by clinical features and CSF findings. In bacterial meningitis, rapid deterioration can occur; early recognition is critical.
b: Mild: fever, headache, no focal signs

sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa, the leading causes of meningitis are bacterial (especially *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Neisseria meningitidis*), tuberculous, and viral (enteroviruses).
b: Post‑vaccination meningitis – pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b

sections.p: Classic triad: fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status. In children, irritability, bulging fontanelle, vomiting. In TB, chronic headache, weight loss, night sweats.
Basic CSF analysis is essential. When advanced tests are unavailable, rely on Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen tests. Blood cultures and CRP guide systemic infection.
b: Microscopy of CSF – for parasites in endemic areas

sections.p: Contraindications include raised ICP (signs: papilledema, focal deficits), coagulopathy, local infection, and severe thrombocytopenia. Complications: post‑LP headache, bleeding, infection, herniation.
b: Post‑LP headache – advise lying flat, hydration

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause promptly. Empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis, antitubercular therapy for TB, antifungals for cryptococcal. Supportive care includes fluids, seizure control, and monitoring ICP.
b: Monitor vitals, glucose, electrolytes, and repeat CSF if clinical decline

sections.p: Repeat CSF when clinically indicated. Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib, and influenza reduces incidence. Counsel on HIV prevention and TB screening.
b: Educate on hand hygiene and avoiding crowded settings

sections.p: Meningitis can mimic viral encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and metabolic encephalopathy. CSF findings help differentiate.
Low CSF glucose can be seen in TB and fungal meningitis; normal glucose does not exclude bacterial meningitis in neonates. Protein may be normal early in viral meningitis.
b: TB meningitis – CSF glucose may be low but not <20 mg/dL

whenToSeekHelp: Severe headache with vomiting and papilledema

faq.q: When is a lumbar puncture contraindicated?
faq.a: When there is suspected raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, focal deficits), coagulopathy, local infection, or severe thrombocytopenia.

faq.q: What is the first step if bacterial meningitis is suspected?
faq.a: Start empirical antibiotics immediately, then perform a lumbar puncture if the patient is stable and no contraindications.

faq.q: Why is dexamethasone added to treatment?
faq.a: It reduces inflammatory damage and improves outcomes in bacterial meningitis, especially with pneumococcus.

exam: What is the most urgent step in a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis and a normal CT? — Start empirical antibiotics before LP; then perform LP if no contraindications.
Which CSF finding differentiates bacterial from viral meningitis? — Neutrophil predominance and high opening pressure in bacterial; lymphocyte predominance and normal pressure in viral.
Why is a lumbar puncture avoided in a patient with papilledema? — Papilledema indicates raised ICP; LP could precipitate herniation.
What is the rationale for adding dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis? — It reduces inflammatory response and lowers mortality.
How would you manage a patient with suspected tuberculous meningitis in a setting without PCR? — Start RIPE therapy empirically and obtain CSF for culture and acid-fast stain; treat for 6–12 months.
Which rapid test is most useful for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV patients? — Cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay; positive result confirms diagnosis.
